metadata.title: Teacher mentorship and job satisfaction: A cross-national econometric analysis of mentees and mentors

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses TALIS 2018 teacher microdata covering lower secondary education (ISCED 2), with a total of 123,299 teachers nested in 8,848 schools across 54 regions/language settings. The authors describe TALIS as collected using a two-stage stratified sampling design with quality assurance, but they do not report applying TALIS design weights in the regression and meta-analytic steps. For inference, they cluster standard errors at the school level and, following OECD guidance for multilevel models, they run unweighted individual regional regressions with school fixed effects; they explicitly note that TALIS replicate weights are mainly intended for descriptive statistics. Therefore, the analysis relies on clustered standard errors and fixed effects rather than weight-based estimation, which may affect population-representativeness and variance estimation relative to fully design-weighted approaches.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This paper models teacher job satisfaction as a continuous Likert-scale score from TALIS and does not involve cognitive achievement plausible values (PVs). As a result, PV handling is not applicable. The manuscript also does not describe any explicit missing-data strategy (e.g., complete-case restriction or imputation), so the missing-data handling is a reporting gap; this matters because TALIS item nonresponse can affect both the first-stage probit (mentor status) and the second-stage job satisfaction equation.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used TALIS 2018 lower secondary (ISCED 2) teacher sample with 123,299 teachers across 8,848 schools and 54 regions/language settings. For the meta-analytic step, the authors excluded 5 regions with fewer than 250 observations to ensure sufficient degrees of freedom, leaving 49 regions treated as independent studies. They also report a robustness re-run excluding 293 mentees who did not yet hold a formal teaching qualification (i.e., removing most pre-service mentoring cases). No additional missing-data rule (e.g., complete-case) is explicitly described in the provided text.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 Lower secondary (ISCED 2) teacher job satisfaction (54 regions/language settings)
main_findings.target_variable: Teacher job satisfaction (continuous Likert score, 0–20) — having a mentor
main_findings.performance_metrics: Two-stage control-function + school fixed effects; random-effects meta-analysis across 49 regions. Overall effect (having a mentor): 0.13 (95% CI [0.09; 0.16]); heterogeneity I² ≈ 0% and Q(47)=47.18, p=0.47. Robustness (excluding 293 unqualified mentees): overall effect 0.12 (95% CI [0.09; 0.16]). Pooled regression (all regions in one model): +0.05 increase (95% CI [0.01; 0.09]).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 lower secondary (ISCED 2) teacher the study leveraged having a mentor alongside teacher self-efficacy, teacher-student relations, and stress-related controls to predict teacher job satisfaction, finding that having a mentor was positively associated with job satisfaction with an overall random-effects effect of 0.13 (95% CI [0.09; 0.16]) and essentially no heterogeneity (I² ≈ 0%). This indicates that implementing or expanding formal mentoring structures for mentees is likely to improve teacher well-being broadly across diverse national contexts, though the cross-sectional design limits causal interpretation.

main_findings.dataset_used: TALIS 2018 Lower secondary (ISCED 2) teacher job satisfaction (54 regions/language settings)
main_findings.target_variable: Teacher job satisfaction (continuous Likert score, 0–20) — being a mentor
main_findings.performance_metrics: Two-stage control-function + school fixed effects; random-effects meta-analysis across 49 regions. Overall effect (being a mentor): 0.82 (95% CI [0.62; 1.02]); heterogeneity I² = 56.1% and Q(47)=110.29, p≈0.00. Robustness (excluding 293 unqualified mentees): overall effect 0.83 (95% CI [0.63; 1.03]). Pooled regression (all regions in one model): +1.01 (95% CI [0.86; 1.15]).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using TALIS 2018 lower secondary (ISCED 2) teacher the study leveraged being a mentor alongside teacher self-efficacy, teacher-student relations, and workload/stress-related controls to predict teacher job satisfaction, finding that serving as a mentor was positively associated with job satisfaction with an overall random-effects effect of 0.82 (95% CI [0.62; 1.02]) but with substantial cross-regional heterogeneity (I² = 56.1%). This indicates that mentor roles can improve mentors’ well-being, yet policy should tailor mentoring implementation (e.g., workload/time/incentives) to local conditions to avoid context-dependent burdens, while causality cannot be fully established from cross-sectional self-reports.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses TALIS 2018 lower secondary (ISCED 2) teacher data (123,299 teachers in 8,848 schools across 54 regions/language settings) to examine whether teachers’ job satisfaction is associated with (i) having a mentor and (ii) being a mentor. The authors apply a two-stage econometric control-function approach to address self-selection into mentoring roles: a first-stage probit for mentor status followed by a second-stage job satisfaction equation with school fixed effects and school-clustered standard errors. They then treat 49 remaining regions (after excluding regions with <250 observations) as independent studies and aggregate region-specific effects using random-effects meta-analysis with inverse-variance weighting. Results show a consistent positive association for mentees (effect 0.13, 95% CI [0.09; 0.16], I² ≈ 0%) and a stronger but more heterogeneous association for mentors (effect 0.82, 95% CI [0.62; 1.02], I² = 56.1%). Limitations include cross-sectional self-reported measures and no explicit missing-data strategy reported; additionally, the analysis is not a machine-learning predictive pipeline.
